At Kew, she was instrumental in organizing and cataloging the vast collection of plant specimens, which included many exotic species brought back from expeditions around the world. Her meticulous documentation and classification methods were revolutionary for the time, helping to establish a standardized system that is still used today.

Myles's work extended beyond mere organization; she was also a prolific writer, authoring several influential books on plant anatomy and physiology. Her most notable work, "The Anatomy of Plants," published in 1815, was a comprehensive guide that detailed the structure and function of different plant parts, greatly advancing the field of botany.

Elara Myles's dedication to science and her innovative approach to botanical research earned her respect and admiration from both her contemporaries and future generations of scientists. Despite facing significant gender-based barriers in her career, she remained steadfast in her pursuit of knowledge, leaving behind a legacy that continues to inspire botanists and naturalists worldwide.
